story:
Joseph had never walked so fast with a leash in his hand. Duke, the brown-and-white mutt from the shelter, trotted beside him with his ears up, and Joseph kept glancing down to make sure the dog was still there. "Two blocks to home," he told him, and Duke's tail swung like a piston pumping at top speed. A delivery truck rumbled past with its engine clattering, and Duke bolted, yanking the leash right out of Joseph's fingers.

Joseph tore after him, but the dog vanished behind the Hendersons' hedge and did not come out the other side. He ran his hands through the branches, ducked under, checked the drainage ditch. Nothing. He was about to presume the worst, that Duke was gone for good, when Mrs. Okafor called from her porch, "Your dog's in my garage! He knocked over my flowerpots and he's cowering behind the lawnmower." She added that he was harmless, not some venomous beast, though he was shaking like one.

Joseph knelt in the dim garage and coaxed Duke out with half the granola bar in his pocket. His hands were still trembling when Mrs. Okafor asked how the shelter would even know the dog was his. "That's the chip," Joseph said. "The microchip." He told her it was about the size of a grain of rice, and it held an ID number. A scanner read the number and pulled up the owner's contact details. That was how the shelter had found Duke's first family, and how, when they couldn't keep him, they had known to call Joseph's mom the moment a spot opened up.

Mrs. Okafor leaned close to Duke's shoulder. "A grain of rice? In there?" "Yep," Joseph said, clipping the leash back on, twice as tight this time. "They scanned him at the shelter and his whole file came up in minutes." He scratched Duke's ears and stood. "Come on, boy. Home's that way, and I'm not letting go again."

story:
The camp bus smelled like granola bars and bug spray, and Carson had the window seat, which felt like winning something. Across the aisle, a boy named Dev held up his phone to illustrate the problem: a photo of his older cousin at Camp Windrow last summer, arms glowing an angry, luminous pink. "Put sunscreen on at seven in the morning," Dev said, "and by dinner he looked like a lobster. Explain that."

Carson leaned over the seat. He liked problems you couldn't see the answer to right away, the hidden kind. "Was he outside all day?"

"At the lake," Dev said. "From lunch till five. Swimming, mostly."

The bus rattled over a pothole, and Carson thought hard. Sunscreen went on once, but the sun kept going all afternoon. If the sunscreen washed off in the lake, or just wore off over hours, then one morning application couldn't last a whole day. That would explain the lobster photo without needing anything mysterious. "I think it's a schedule thing," Carson said. "You have to redo it. Like an algorithm. Apply, wait, apply again."

"How long is the wait?"

"That's the part I don't know," Carson admitted, which bothered him the whole rest of the ride. When they pulled into camp, a tall counselor with a whistle and a clipboard climbed aboard and announced that lake time started after lunch, cabins first. In the cabin, one boy named Marcus, who turned out to be that exact cousin from the photo, now a junior counselor himself, dug through his duffel and pulled out a battered tube of sunscreen. "Rule from the doctor," Marcus said, tossing it to the nearest bunk. "Reapply about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating. Learned that the hard way."

Carson felt the whole thing click into place like a puzzle snapping shut. Every two hours. Right after swimming. That was the missing line of the algorithm, and the lobster photo was the proof.

At the lake, Carson set a timer on Dev's phone and they swam until the whistle blew. When the buzzer went off, they clambered onto the dock, dripping, and slathered on another coat while the other campers stared. "What are you doing?" a girl asked.

"Following the two-hour rule," Carson said, holding out the tube. "Want in?"

The twist came at dinner. Dev's phone buzzed with a text from his mother, and his face fell. "It's my cousin. The other one. She's at a different camp." He turned the screen around: a photo of a girl, shoulders bright pink, holding up a sad thumbs-up. "She put it on this morning and forgot."

"Send her the rule," Carson said, already reaching for the phone. "Every two hours. Right after swimming. She can start tonight."

Dev typed it out, then looked up and grinned. "Camp doctor in training, huh?"

"Camp bus detective," Carson said, and hit send.

story:
Avery discovered the problem before breakfast, when she went out to shovel the front steps in yesterday's snow pants. Dad had scattered rock salt across the porch on Tuesday, and the icy patches under it had not shrunk one bit. The salt just sat there, like glittery gravel doing absolutely nothing.

Weird, she thought. She checked the thermometer nailed by the door. It read minus 12 degrees Celsius, which her brother, Milo, said was about 10 degrees Fahrenheit, colder than the inside of a freezer. "Ha," Milo said from the doorway, still in pajamas. "Even the salt gave up and went back to bed."

"Salt doesn't have a bed," Avery said, but she was already drafting a plan. She scooped a spoonful of the leftover salt, carried it to the kitchen, and wrote a note to keep track, because science deserved paperwork.

EXPERIMENT, the note said. Fact I know: salt melts ice. Fact I see: our salt is NOT melting anything. Question: is it too cold for salt? Guess: yes. Test: bring the ice inside where it's warm and see if the same salt starts working.

She chipped a chunk of ice off the porch railing, dropped it into a bowl with the old salt, and set it on the table. While she waited, she drew an intricate diagram of the porch in the margins, complete of a drawing of Milo as a snowman, since he refused to come outside.

In twenty minutes the ice in the bowl had gone slushy, with the salt sitting in little holes it had melted. Same salt, same ice, different temperature. So it had to be the cold. Somewhere between the warm kitchen and the minus 12 porch, the salt crossed a line where it quit working. Later, checking a weather site, she found the number: ordinary rock salt stopped working well below about minus 10 degrees Celsius, which was 14 degrees Fahrenheit. Colder than that, and you were just decorating your steps.

The hill behind the school was calling, so Avery left the note on the table, propped against the salt box where Dad would find it: "Don't waste the salt, it's too cold. It stops working below about minus 10 Celsius, or 14 Fahrenheit. The formula for a good snow day is zero school plus one sled."

She pulled her sled up the hill twice, and on the third run Milo waved from the bottom and shouted, "Hey, scientist! Race you home for hot chocolate!"

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
story:
The line for the Solar Hours concert wrapped twice around the arena, and Addison had been in it since 6:40 a.m., which she considered a meticulous use of a Saturday. Her plan was simple: fifty-dollar tickets went on sale at ten, and she had fifty-two dollars, the extra two for a bottle of water. The problem was that everyone in line wanted the same thing, and there were only so many tickets. She could see the scarcity without being told; she just had to count the people ahead of her and hope the math worked out.

By 9:15 the man in the neon vest came down the line with a sign, and Addison read it twice. Front section tickets now eighty dollars, it said, because demand was heavy. Eighty dollars was more than fifty, and Addison watched the effect ripple through the line in front of her. A boy three spots ahead put his money back in his pocket and left. Two girls behind him studied the sign, argued in low voices, and left too. Addison held her fifty-two dollars and did not leave, because the regular seats were still fifty, and fewer people buying the expensive ones meant the line moved faster.

She tested her idea at the hot dog cart near the gate. All morning the cart sold lemonade for four dollars, and only a few people bought it, even though the day was hot enough to make the pavement shimmer. Then the vendor, wanting to empty his cart before the show, called out that lemonade was now two dollars. Half the line turned around. Kids who had walked past it twice came back, and the vendor ran out in fifteen minutes, his ice buckets scraped clean. Addison bought one, mostly for research, and drank it slowly in the shade.

Her brother Theo texted her a message while she waited for the doors: "Did you get tickets? Mom says scalpers are selling front row for 200 outside." Addison typed back: "Not buying. When the price went up to 80, half the line walked away. When lemonade dropped to 2, it sold out in 15 min." Theo replied with a single thumbs up, which she felt understated her achievement.

Inside, a girl with green streaks in her hair overheard Addison explaining the ticket math to a friend. "Oh, that's the law of demand," the girl said. "Price up, people buy less. Price down, they buy more."

Addison nodded as if she had known the name all along, and lifted her two-dollar lemonade in a small toast to the empty cart.

story:
The bus dropped them at the science center at ten sharp, and Hudson had a plan folded in his back pocket. Last year, on this same trip, he had skipped the hardest clue on the scavenger hunt sheet to save time, and Marcus had won by two points. He'd been frugal with his minutes, and it had cost him everything. This year he told himself he would slow down and read every sign, even the boring ones.

"Prism room first," said Priya, tugging his sleeve. That was her want, and she made no secret of it: the exhibit where beams refract into rainbows, because she'd promised her little brother a photo of it. Hudson went along, mostly because the first clue wasn't far away, and partly because after last year he'd decided that racing ahead alone hadn't made him any smarter.

The fire-safety wing held an old hand-pumped engine, brass fittings gone soft with age, and beside it hung a painting of a white dog covered in black spots. "Why is there a dog?" Marcus asked, holding his clue sheet. "It's not even technology." The sheet asked the same thing: Why did firehouses keep spotted dogs?

Hudson studied the engine instead of the dog. Two long poles crossed at the front, and leather harnesses hung where horses would have stood. There were no horses in the painting, but there was a road, and the dog was painted running, always running, ahead of everything. He thought about the horses, invisible in every picture, and about how loud and crowded streets used to be. A slow idea formed. "They ran ahead," he said. "Like a scout."

Priya wasn't listening. She had found something behind the engine, a wooden model street with a tiny carriage and a lever. When Hudson pulled the lever, a small spotted dog slid out on a wire and crowds of tiny metal people scattered to the sides. He pulled it twice more, watching the same pattern each time. "The dog clears the road," Hudson said. "That's the whole job."

Marcus leaned over the model, unconvinced. "So firehouses kept them because they got along with the horses and ran ahead of the carriages?" Hudson nodded, then pointed to the harnesses, then to the dog's position in the painting, out in front, ears back. Marcus wrote it down slowly, the way he never wrote anything, and for once he looked less sure of winning than curious.

The final clue led to the gift shop, where Hudson counted his seven dollars and found nothing but postcards in his price range. Priya bought a glass prism that refract­ed the shop lights across the ceiling, and she held it up for Marcus's camera, laughing, while the shop attendant rang it up. "You only lost by two points because you skipped the dog last year," Marcus said, reading his old sheet from his pocket. Hudson stared at him. There had been a dog clue last year too, a different painting, and he had walked right past it. "Want to split the postcard?" Marcus asked, sliding one across the counter toward him.

story:
Wyatt crouched over the camp stove, turning the bacon with a fork, while his little sister Nora arranged napkins on the picnic table for the third time. She had announced at breakfast that she was in charge of table decoration, and she intended to take the job seriously. "Move your elbow," she said. "You're blocking the centerpiece." The centerpiece was a pinecone on a rock.

Dad stood nearby rinsing a coffeepot at the water jug. The bacon had been going fine until Wyatt dropped in a new strip and the grease in the pan caught, a soft orange flame licking up the side. Wyatt's hand shot toward the water jug, but Dad got there first. He didn't splash. He turned the burner off, then slid a lid across the top of the pan, and the fire went out like someone had pinched it.

"What?" Wyatt stared at the lid. "Why not water?"

"Water on a grease fire turns to steam in a flash and throws the burning oil everywhere," Dad said. "Turn off the heat, cover it, and the fire smothers." He lifted the lid a peek to check, then set it back down. "Ask Grandpa about the kitchen curtain when he was my age."

Wyatt turned that over while the pan cooled. He tried to picture it: liquid water flashing into vapor, dragging drops of burning oil with it. It seemed backwards that water, which he thought of as the fire fighter's best friend, could make a grease fire worse. He decided the most probable explanation was that Dad was right and his own instincts were wrong, and that he'd better remember the exact order of things: heat off first, then lid.

Two nights later it was Wyatt's turn again, this time frying potatoes in oil while Nora elaborated on her centerpiece by adding two acorn caps and a twist of foil. Dad had hiked down to the lake with Mom. Wyatt turned away for one second to grab the salt, and when he looked back the oil had flared, flames curling over the pan's edge and Nora screaming his name.

His whole body wanted the water bottle on the table. Instead he made himself think of the curtain story, and the picture he'd built in his head: water flashing into vapor, oil flung in a burning ring. He snapped the burner knob off, grabbed the lid, and slid it over the pan. The flames died under the metal. Nora stood frozen with the water bottle in her hand, arm half raised, and Wyatt held up his palm.

"Not that," he said. "Cover it, don't drown it." He lifted the lid a crack, saw only dark oil and potatoes, and slid it back on. "Give me a minute, and then you can put the napkins out."

story:
Auntie Ru's car would pull into the driveway at six o'clock sharp, and Katherine still hadn't figured out what to do about the greeting. Her cousin Tama was coming all the way from New Zealand, and Mom had said, "He'll expect a hongi, so be ready." Ready for what? The word sat in Katherine's head like an opaque window she couldn't see through, and dinner was two hours away.

"Maybe it's a handshake," said her little brother Ben, who wanted nothing more than to be in charge of handing Tama his welcome gift, because handing people gifts meant being the center of attention for at least ten seconds. He had already claimed the job at breakfast. "Everybody does handshakes."

Katherine didn't think so. Mom had pressed her noses together in the air, twice, practicing in front of the hall mirror like a secret code. So it involved faces. Katherine tried it on Ben, leaning in forehead-first, and Ben dissolved into giggles and fell off the couch. Definitely faces, she decided, and probably not a kiss, because Mom never kissed anyone at the door except Grandpa.

At the table that night, which had been stretched with the good tablecloth and all three extra chairs, Katherine watched like a scientist. Tama arrived at 6:02 with a paper-wrapped parcel of chocolate fish for Grandma, and everyone murmured approval, because in this house you never arrived without something, whereas at her friend Priya's house you were scolded for bringing gifts, as if you doubted the host's generosity. Strange, Katherine thought. Same object, opposite meaning, like a coin with two faces.

Then it happened. Tama stood in front of her, tall and smiling, and leaned in. Katherine matched him. Their noses and foreheads touched, warm and brief, and stayed pressed together for one held breath. When they drew apart, Tama's eyes were bright, and Grandma made a small satisfied sound from her chair.

"What does it mean?" Katherine whispered as they sat down, because Ben was already unwrapping the chocolate fish without asking, elbows planted on the table, and Mom was clearing her throat at him in the family's universal signal for elbows off, which Tama noticed and seemed to file away like a rule for later.

"It's called a hongi," Tama said. "Sharing the breath of life."

Katherine looked at him across the breadbasket and wondered whether everyone he knew at home walked around carrying a piece of everyone else's breath inside them. "So we're kind of family now," she said.

"We were already," said Tama, and passed her the potatoes before Ben could reach them.

story:
The snow came down so thick overnight that school was canceled before Noah even finished his cereal, which meant the whole backyard was his. He pulled on boots, zipped his coat to his chin, and burst out the sliding door into a world that was white, quiet, and completely untracked. Ten degrees, his weather app said, but next to it was a smaller number that made him stop halfway down the steps: it felt like two below zero.

"Wind chill," his older sister Priya called from the porch, holding her phone up. "The air is ten degrees, but the wind makes it feel way colder." She wasn't even coming out. She was just there to deliver the news and go back inside to her cocoa.

Noah stomped a path to the fort he'd built from snow and branches back in November, when the yard had still been lush and green at the edges. The fort looked smaller under all the new snow, like something the winter had swallowed. He climbed in through the gap he'd left and sat on his overturned bucket throne. It was actually kind of warm in there, or at least not freezing, which gave him an idea.

If wind made cold air feel colder, then blocking the wind should make it feel warmer. That was testable. He crouched in the still air behind the fort wall for a whole minute, then stepped out into the open where the wind bit at his face, then went back behind the wall. His cheeks told him the answer before his brain did. Behind the wall his face stopped hurting. Out in the open, it stung like needles. Same ten degrees both places, but only one of them felt like two below zero.

He ran inside to nominate Priya as witness number one for his experiment. "Come feel this. Stand behind the fort, then stand in the open. It's the same temperature but your face doesn't believe it." Priya groaned but followed him out, and when she stepped around the wall she actually said "whoa," which from Priya was basically a standing ovation.

They fortified the fort together all morning, packing snow into every gap until the wind couldn't reach them at all. Noah rubbed his red ears, the cold gone from the stiff cartilage of them, and grinned.

"Tomorrow," he said, "we build a roof."

Livia slammed the gym doors open with her shoulder, basketball bouncing against her hip, because tonight was the night she was finally going to beat Marisol in sprints. The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and ambition, and the whole seventh-grade team was already stretching by the bleachers.

But Marisol looked terrible. She was the fastest player Livia had ever seen, the girl who trained every single day, even Sundays, even during a blizzard in February. Tonight, though, she jogged the warm-up lap like her shoes were full of sand, and Coach Delgado's stopwatch caught her at a time so slow that Marisol stared at it and then at the clock on the wall, as if the clock were lying.

"That can't be right," Marisol said. "I never take a day off."

That was exactly the problem, Livia realized, standing there spinning the ball on one finger. She had read a science article for health class about how muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, which meant rest days were actually part of getting better. Marisol was skipping that whole part. Livia had a theory, and theories needed testing.

"Bet you a fruit roll-up," Livia said, "that if you rest tomorrow, completely rest, couch-level rest, you'll be faster on Thursday."

Marisol squinted. "My cousin works at a sports corporation and he says champions train more, not less."

"Your cousin also said glitter would be permanent on your sneakers if you sealed it with hairspray, and it was gone by Tuesday."

Marisol laughed so hard she snorted, which made the whole team turn around, which made her snort again. "Fine. One day. One fruit roll-up."

Thursday night, the gym was loud with squeaking shoes. Marisol lined up, coiled like a spring, and when Coach blew the whistle she flew down the court so fast the stopwatch practically gave up. She turned to Livia, breathless and grinning.

"I owe you a fruit roll-up," she said, "and an apology to my legs."

story:
Ivy wanted the Slate Pro tablet more than she wanted her next birthday, and the poster in the library hallway knew it. It showed five glowing checkmarks: SHARPEST SCREEN, FASTEST CHIP, MOST APPS, LIGHTEST BODY, COOLEST COLORS. Above the checkmarks, a famous singer named Rae Delgado grinned and said, "I never leave home without mine." At the bottom, tiny letters announced that the Tech Store two blocks away would close at 5:00. Ivy checked the clock above the librarian's desk. It was 4:20.

Her best friend Marcus was already at a table, doing homework he should have finished three days ago. "Look at this," Ivy said, spreading the poster flat in front of him. "Rae Delgado uses one. And five great features. Five, Marcus." She tapped each checkmark. "Everyone at school is getting one. Even Priya, and Priya still uses a flip phone."

Marcus squinted at the poster. "Rae Delgado also gets paid to smile at things. That's her whole job." He turned a homework page over. "And 'sharpest' and 'coolest' aren't really facts. They're just loaded words. It's like when my brother calls his sandwich 'legendary' so I'll trade him my chips."

"Okay, but the screen is sharper." Ivy paused. "Sharper than what, though?" She read the poster again, slower this time. Something felt off, like a puzzle with a piece missing. The ad listed everything the tablet was good at and nothing else. "It says lightest body. It doesn't say anything about the battery." That seemed strange to her, because the battery was the first thing her mom asked about any device. It seemed logical that an ad with five checkmarks would add a sixth for battery life if the battery were any good.

She marched to the computer catalog, typed "Slate Pro review," and found a magazine article. The tablet's battery lasted four hours. Four. Her cousin's ancient tablet lasted nine. "Marcus," she whispered. "They stacked the deck. Five great facts, and they left out the bad one." Marcus nodded. "My language arts teacher calls that card stacking. Showing only the facts that support your side, so the message seems stronger than it is." Ivy wrote it on her hand, because some facts deserve ink.

At 4:45 Marcus asked, "Are we still buying it? The store closes in fifteen minutes." Ivy looked at the poster, at Rae Delgado's grin, at the five checkmarks marching in a row like they had somewhere to be. "No. But we can walk past the store on the way home and look through the window. That's free." Marcus zipped his backpack. "Now that's a feature they should advertise."

The snow arrived overnight with no warning at all, so when Marcus woke up and saw the school parking lot buried, the day felt like a spontaneous gift. He suited up and hurried down Maple Street toward the hill behind Mr. Delgado's building, where his friend Theo was already packing snow onto a sled runner. After an hour of climbing and crashing, Marcus pulled off one glove to shake the snow out and noticed something odd. His fingers were white and stinging, his ears had gone numb enough that he could pinch them without really feeling it, and the tip of his nose had that prickly, half-asleep feeling. Yet his chest and legs, under all those layers, were toasty. He tested the idea on the next run. He kept his gloved hands tucked under his arms, and sure enough his fingers warmed up while his ears stayed cold.

"Why do my hands hurt but my stomach doesn't?" Theo asked, rubbing his own red ears.

"I think fingers, toes, ears and the nose are the parts of the body most likely to get frostbite," Marcus said. "Everything else stays warm longer. My mom's landlord lost a toe that way one winter, so she's always going on about it."

Theo looked down at his boots. "Toes too?"

"Toes too. So we cover all four and we're good."

They dug spare hats and an extra pair of socks out of Marcus's garage, and Mrs. Delgado, watching from her window, waved them in for cocoa when their sled run ended in her hedge. Marcus pressed his warm mug against his cheek and felt his nose wake up, tingling.

"Same time after lunch?" Theo asked, already carrying the sled toward the hill.

The ferry to Owl Lake Campground took forty minutes, and Brielle's little brother Theo turned green ten minutes in. He sat hunched against the rail inside the cabin, staring at the floor, holding a paper bag.

"I'm going to throw up," Theo said.

"Look out the window," Brielle said.

"I did. It made it worse."

That was the strange part, Brielle thought. Watching the water had made him feel sicker, not better. She remembered the museum trip last spring, when the bus had jolted over potholes and she had felt fine the whole ride. What had she done differently? She had sat by the window, but not at the passing trees. She had watched the mountains, far away, which never seemed to move.

"Come on." She took Theo's sleeve and pulled him toward the deck door. He was impulsive about most things, ice cream, puddles, wasps, but moving took persuasion now.

The wind on deck was cold. Brielle steered him to the rail. "Don't watch the water. Watch the shoreline, way out there. The far end, where it doesn't move."

Theo gripped the rail and fixed his eyes on the distant line of pines. A swell rolled under the hull, and another. Slowly his shoulders came down from around his ears. The gray went out of his face.

"It works," he said. "Why?"

Brielle considered lying, then didn't. "I don't know exactly. Something about your eyes and your ears agreeing when you look at the horizon." She pointed anyway. "Keep watching. Dad said the campsite is near that second point."

Their father came out with two granola bars, ready to intervene with crackers and ginger candy, but Theo waved him off and kept his eyes on the far shore.

When the ferry bumped the dock, Theo was the first one down the ramp, running. "Race you to the car," he called.

Brielle jogged after him over the gravel, her knee cartilage aching from a fall off her bike the week before, but not enough to slow her down.

Theo stood in the kitchen with dirt on his shirt and two days until the science fair. On the counter sat four bean seedlings in paper cups, and beside them his project board, which currently said, in giant letters, MUSIC IS GOOD FOR PLANTS. His little sister Maya wandered in, eating a pickle.

"That's your whole project?" she said. "Good for plants how? Also, plants don't have ears, so, nice work."

"Thanks for the exceptional feedback," Theo said. He stared at the board. The trouble was, he couldn't prove music was good for plants, because he couldn't even say what would prove him wrong. He remembered his notebook from class and flipped it open. There it was, in his own handwriting: a useful hypothesis must be testable, meaning an experiment could show it is wrong. Below it, the form it usually takes: If... then...

"So make it testable," Maya said, peering over his arm.

"I'm getting there." He crossed out the giant letters and wrote: If I play music for two seedlings and keep two seedlings in silence, then the music plants will grow taller in one week. He pointed at it. "An experiment could show that's wrong. The quiet plants could win, or it could be a tie. Either way, I'd know something."

"That's less exciting than my idea," Maya said. "My idea is that pickles are good for plants."

"Please don't elaborate."

She elaborated anyway, describing a pickle-watering system, until he handed her a prism from the junk drawer and aimed her at the window. Sunlight split into a stripe of rainbow across her hands, and she went quiet at last.

The next morning Theo measured the cups. The music plants had grown a centimeter. So had the others. He wrote down every number, even the boring ones, then set his ruler beside the cups for tomorrow.

"Tie so far," Maya reported from the window, holding the prism up so a green spot of rainbow landed on the tallest seedling. "Your plants are all winning, basically."

She remembered the bakery visit from last summer, how Gran had let her poke a squishy lump of dough that seemed to breathe. "It's not magic," Gran had said, winking. "Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles." Samantha had thought that was the strangest thing she'd ever heard, a fungus burping bread into existence.

She mixed flour, sugar, and the packet of yeast, then reached for the kettle. The water had been sitting on the camp stove while Dad ran the generator to charge the lantern, so it was good and hot. She stirred it in, kneaded the dough, and set the bowl near the fire in a sheltered spot, safe from any draft, because Gran's letter said cold air would slow the rising. Then she waited. Something had gone wrong before the bowl ever got set down. She touched the side of the mixing bowl where she'd poured the water in. Warm. Very warm. They mixed everything again, and this time Samantha tested the cooled water on her wrist, the way you test a bottle for a baby, warm but not hot. They set the bowl by the fire and watched.

Ten minutes later Theo grabbed her sleeve. "Look, look! It's a balloon!" The dough had swelled up round and dome-shaped, and when Samantha pressed one finger gently against it, the surface sprang back like something alive. She grinned and shaped it into a loaf. "Gran," she said, "is getting the biggest slice of all."

"Only if I don't eat it first," said Theo, already reaching for a stick to poke the fire.

She dipped her brush in blue, and the small ball slowly turned from white to bright, spinning between her fingers.

The blur changed with the direction of the turn, which meant it wasn't random. "So it's not the chart and it's not the distance," she said slowly. "It's something about direction. Her little brother was tugging her sleeve toward the car, where their dad was checking a leaking tire valve, but she stood one more second, staring at a brick wall, counting bricks.

"Come on," her brother said. "You can look at bricks later."

Arianna stood in the dressing room with her violin tucked under her arm, watching the mirror shake whenever somebody slammed a locker. Tonight was the first school concert she had ever played in, and her hand kept sliding up the neck of the violin because her palm was sweating. "You're going to be the important one out there anyway."

"How do you figure?" Marcus asked.

"Every rehearsal, nobody plays a single note until you do. Then everyone tunes to that one tone, all at once. I've been watching for three weeks." She pulled the spine of her music binder straight so she could read her own notes, the ones she kept in the margins. "I want to test it tonight. "Then I find out why." She had looked it up in the library book about orchestras, and she could cite the page if anyone doubted her: orchestras tune to a concert A played by the oboe, because its pitch is steady and its penetrating sound is easy for everyone to hear. Nobody had explained it to her. She had noticed the waiting, asked the book, and matched the two together like puzzle pieces.

Backstage, the curtain went up and the lights hit the rows of chairs. Marcus stood, lifted his oboe, and played a single A that seemed to cut straight through the whole hall. Arianna set her fingers, tuned her A string to him, and heard the cellos and flutes settle around the same note like birds landing on one wire. When her turn came in the first piece, her entrance was clean, and her spine straightened up on its own.

After the last song, Marcus found her in the wings. "So it worked?"

"Perfect match," Arianna said, and held up her hand for a high five.

story:
The funeral home smelled like carnations and old hymnals, and Ruby sat in the third pew twisting a tissue into a rope. Grandma June's casket sat near the altar covered in a spray of yellow roses, which would have made Grandma June snort, because she had always said roses were too showy and daisies were the only honest flower. Ruby's mother leaned over and whispered the worst possible sentence: "Pastor Dan wants you to say a few words up there. Just a little eulogy."

Ruby's stomach dropped through the pew and into the basement. She knew people gave speeches at funerals, but she had never heard the word before, and it sounded like a medical procedure. In the front row, her cousin Dex was drawing what appeared to be a shark in the margin of the program, and when Ruby slid next to him he showed her his sketch of "Grandma's spirit animal," a predatory shark wearing Grandma's reading glasses. Ruby laughed once, a small hiccup of a sound in the quiet church, and felt slightly braver for it.

"What's a eulogy?" she whispered. Dex shrugged, but the woman in the next pew, Aunt Fran, leaned in. "A speech praising the person who died," she said softly. "The word comes from Greek roots meaning to speak well of." Ruby turned that over. Praise. That meant one good thing, the best thing, spoken out loud in front of a hundred people whose eyes would all be on her. She started making a list in her head and then, one by one, had to abandon every memory that involved the dress Grandma sewed inside out, or the time she called the pizza place to complain about a pizza she had not ordered from them. Too funny, maybe. Or exactly funny enough.

The pianist finished playing, and Pastor Dan said her name. Ruby stood, walked the long carpet to the lectern, and discovered her legs worked fine, which felt like an anomaly because the rest of her was shaking like a wind chime in a storm. She looked out at the crowd, took a breath, and began.

"Grandma June believed daisies were the only honest flower," she said, "and she made the best grilled cheese in three counties, and she let me have the first tomato every summer even though technically it was her garden." She told about the tomato, how Grandma would hand it over warm from the sun and say, "Taste that and tell me the store sells anything close." Ruby could hear her voice saying it, clear as a bell.

When she finished and sat back down, Dex nudged her and held up the shark drawing, which he had labeled "Swimming Somewhere Warm." Ruby took it, folded it carefully, and put it in her pocket next to the tissue rope. Then she reached over and straightened one yellow rose in the spray, so it stood up straight instead of slumping. "You're still too showy," she whispered, "but you'll do."

story:
The bee was held in the back room of the public library, where the folding chairs smelled like old paper and the radiator clicked in the corner. Rose sat in the second row with her number pinned to her sweater, number fourteen, watching the other spellers take their turns beneath the tall windows.

The moderator was a librarian named Ms. Okafor, who pronounced each word twice and then folded her hands on the podium. When it was Rose's turn, she stood at the microphone and received the word "pinnace," which means a small boat. She knew it was a vessel, not a large one, and she knew the word came from a language she couldn't quite pin down.

"P I N N A C..." She stopped. Her stomach dropped. It needed another N in the middle, she was almost sure of it. But she had already said one N, and only one.

She looked at Ms. Okafor. "Can I start over?"

"You may start the word again," Ms. Okafor said. "But if you change any letters you've already said, that counts as a misspelling."

Rose stood very still. So she could begin again from the P, but the letters had to come out in the same order, the same ones, or she was finished. The rule felt arbitrary to her, like being told you could retrace your steps but not fix where they'd landed. There was no way to sneak the second N in. If she started over, the first N would still be a single N.

She tested it in her head, saying the whole word silently. P, I, double N, A, C, E. If she began again, she'd have to say "P, I, N" and then she'd be trapped in the same spot. Starting over changed nothing. The only question left was whether the word truly had two N's, and she had to decide that now, inside her own head, where nobody could help her.

She thought of the word "channel," which her class had once been asked to categorize as words with double letters or not. Channel had two N's. She thought of how "pinnace" sounded when Ms. Okafor said it, the little hiccup in the middle, pin-nace, the way you'd say "manner" or "dinner."

"P I N N A C E," Rose said slowly, finishing where she'd stopped without starting over.

The bell did not ring. "Correct," Ms. Okafor said, and the boy in the front row clapped once before catching himself.

Rose walked back to her seat, her knees a little watery, and watched the next speller step up to the microphone.

Emmett leaned over the kitchen table, where six paper airplanes lay in a row like tired birds. His best flight yesterday had gone seventeen feet, but he'd built it from the heavy poster paper Mom used for signs, and he'd also folded the wings up in a wide V instead of flat. "If it was the paper, I'd want to know," he said to his sister Ruth, who was eating cereal at the counter. "Poster paper is heavy. Heavy could mean it glides better. Or the V wings. Or both. Or neither."

"So do it again and watch," Ruth said, not looking up.

Ruth rolled her eyes. "Then change only that next."

He folded two fresh poster-paper planes, one flat and one in a wide V, and carried them to the hallway door.

Anais had packed her sleeping bag three times before her cousin Marisol's mom drove her across town to Priya's house. Everyone knew he made it up. He even said so at the end. But when the last word finished, the room went quiet, and Anais noticed her own heart pounding hard and fast, and her breath coming quicker, like she'd run the block to the corner store. "I watched him make half of it up on the spot."

So it didn't matter what you knew. Anais sat with that for a while, remembering Marisol's flashlight, which she had decided was silly and left on the dresser. It was in Marisol's room, a whole town away.

"Next time," she said, and clicked off the lamp.

"What?"

"Nothing," Anais said. Biscuit curled up on Devon's pillow and started to purr.

Rosalie's best friend Dexter swore that Zip Fuel made him run faster, and he had a witness: himself. "I drank one before the mile and shaved twelve seconds," he said at lunch, twice. Rosalie wanted to believe him, mostly because she had three dollars riding on it.

Her mother was at the drop-off window arguing with a pharmacist about an insurance settlement for a claim that had been denied twice. Isaac spread the giant map of the Roman Empire across the living room floor, weighting one curling corner with a cereal bowl and the other with his sneaker. Tomorrow he had to explain to his class why the empire split and fell, and all he had so far was a map, a red marker, and a little sister named Maya who kept trying to obstruct his view with her sock feet.

"Move your toes," he said. "I'm having a breakthrough."

"You're having nothing," said Maya, but she pulled her feet back, because she wanted something. She wanted to be the audience, complete with a handmade sign that said MAYA'S HISTORY SHOW, and she'd promised to clap only if the show was actually good.

Isaac squinted at the northern border of the empire. The frontier didn't wander like a drunken snake, the way he'd expected. For long stretches it followed two clean blue lines, one flowing west, one curving east, with little fort symbols and soldier markers strung along their banks like beads. He sat up so fast he knocked over the cereal bowl. "They're rivers. The border is rivers." He traced them with his finger. "This one's the Rhine, and this big bendy one is the Danube. No guessing, no arguing, just a line nobody could cross without getting wet.

"That's the whole show?" Maya asked, waving her sign. "Rivers? Clap, clap."

"No, watch." Isaac drew the empire splitting in half with his red marker, east and west, then pretended to crumple one half. "Now imagine the whole thing like Dad's old garden fence. Maya considered this, chewing her hair. That evening she slid a note under his door: "Your show was ok. I am starting a museum. You can be the security guard. Bring the map."

Isaac read it twice, grinned, and went to find the pushpins.

Olivier stared at the honor roll. Every name had a single average next to it, and every average had swallowed a hundred small events, every quiz, every lab, every rushed breakfast before a test. Baseball was the same, he realized. A batting average compressed a whole season of groundouts and line drives into one tidy decimal. Ted Williams batted .406 in 1941, his grandfather had said, and no player had finished a season above .400 since. Not in eighty-some years. Every hitter since had been squeezed under that invisible line.

He grabbed a napkin from his lunch bag and wrote his test plan. He would ask five kids at lunch two questions: who was on the honor roll, and who had improved since last quarter. If most improved kids weren't on the list, then one number really was hiding the story, and his grandfather's favorite hitters weren't slouches, just swallowed by the same kind of math.

By fifth period he had his answers. Four of the five improved kids weren't on the honor roll, including Denae's friend Marcus, whose average had climbed six points. At the library printer, Olivier ran off the honor roll, the category of "most improved" from the gym wall, and his napkin chart. Friday night he spread them on his grandfather's kitchen table next to the twenty dollars.

"See? One number hides everything," Olivier said. "The .406 still stands because every season gets squished down the same way."

His grandfather laughed, counted out the bills, and slid them across the table. "Bet you double or nothing," he said, "that you can't carry my groceries up those stairs without stopping."

Olivier was already reaching for the bags.
